Dionysius the Areopagite
dy-oh-NISH-ee-us the air-ee-OP-uh-gyte
proper noun (an Athenian convert)
From Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus council, converted under Paul's preaching at Athens (Acts 17:34); later the falsely-attributed author of the “Pseudo-Dionysian” mystical writings.

📖 Biblical Definition

Dionysius the Areopagite was a member of the Athenian council of the Areopagus who, when most mocked or delayed at Paul's preaching of the resurrection, clave unto the apostle and believed. He stands in Acts as living proof that the gospel reached even the cultured and powerful of Athens—a counsellor of the city among the firstfruits of Greece, alongside the woman Damaris and others. Though not many wise men after the flesh are called, God called this one, that no class of men might think itself beyond the reach of grace. The dictionary honours the historical Dionysius as a true convert and a token of the gospel's power among the learned. It must, however, sharply distinguish him from the body of mystical writings later forged in his name. In the late fifth or early sixth century an unknown author, steeped in Neoplatonism, composed treatises on the divine names, the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies, and mystical theology, and passed them off under the prestige of the apostolic convert. These “Pseudo-Dionysian” writings exercised vast and harmful influence on medieval mysticism, hierarchy, and the doctrine of God, importing a Neoplatonic ladder of being and an apophatic mysticism foreign to Scripture. The dictionary names the forgery for what it is and applies the apostolic rule: prove all things, hold fast that which is good. The true Dionysius is honoured as an Athenian trophy of grace; the writings stolen for his name are weighed by the Word and found wanting, a warning that a venerable name is no guarantee of sound doctrine.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Athenian Areopagite converted under Paul's preaching (Acts 17:34), a trophy of grace among the learned; sharply distinguished from the later Neoplatonic “Pseudo-Dionysian” writings forged in his name, which the dictionary names a forgery to be weighed by the Word.

DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE, proper noun. A member of the Athenian Areopagus, converted under Paul.

He clave to Paul and believed when others mocked the resurrection (Acts 17:34).

A token that the gospel reached the cultured and powerful of Athens.

Not to be confused with the later “Pseudo-Dionysian” mystical writings forged in his name.

Those Neoplatonic forgeries are weighed by the Word and found wanting.

📖 Key Scripture

Ac 17:34 — "Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them."

Ac 17:32 — "And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter."

1 Co 1:26 — "For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:"

1 Th 5:21 — "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The chief corruption is the body of Neoplatonic mystical writings forged in Dionysius's name, which shaped medieval mysticism and hierarchy by importing a ladder of being and apophatic mysticism foreign to Scripture.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the historical Dionysius as a genuine convert and a token of the gospel's power among the learned and powerful of Athens. Though not many wise after the flesh are called, God called this counsellor of the Areopagus, that no class of men might count itself beyond the reach of grace. His conversion is honourable history, and the dictionary receives it as such.

The corruption attaches not to the man but to the forgery done in his name. In the late fifth or early sixth century an anonymous author steeped in Neoplatonism wrote treatises—on the divine names, the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies, and mystical theology—and passed them off under the prestige of the apostolic convert. These “Pseudo-Dionysian” writings shaped medieval mysticism, the hierarchy of angels and church offices, and a heavily apophatic doctrine of God, importing a Neoplatonic ladder of being foreign to Scripture. The dictionary names the forgery plainly and applies the apostolic rule: prove all things, hold fast that which is good. A venerable name is no guarantee of sound doctrine; the writings must be tried by the Word, and where they depart from it, they are to be refused however ancient their false credentials.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Dionysius (a common Greek name, after the god Dionysus) and “Areopagite” (a member of the Areopagus council); the true convert distinguished from the pseudonymous later author.

expand to see more

Dionysios, a Greek name derived from the god Dionysus.

“Areopagite,” a member of the council of the Areopagus (Mars' hill).

Converted under Paul's Athenian sermon (Acts 17:34).

“Pseudo-Dionysius,” the later anonymous Neoplatonist who forged writings in his name.

His name a warning that prestige is no guarantee of sound doctrine.

Usage

"The teacher honoured Dionysius as a trophy of grace among the learned of Athens."

"He distinguished the convert sharply from the Pseudo-Dionysian forgeries of later centuries."

"She weighed the writings stolen for his name by the Word, and found them wanting."
